data.command: What is T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter?

data.text:
T1059 — Command and Scripting Interpreter is a technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under the Execution tactic (TA0002).

Core idea: Adversaries abuse legitimate command-line and scripting interpreters — which exist natively on nearly every platform — to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. Because these interpreters are trusted, signed system components, using them can blend malicious activity into normal administration and help evade defenses that only watch for suspicious standalone executables.

Sub-techniques:

| ID | Interpreter |
|---|---|
| T1059.001 | PowerShell |
| T1059.002 | AppleScript |
| T1059.003 | Windows Command Shell (cmd.exe) |
| T1059.004 | Unix Shell (bash, sh, zsh) |
| T1059.005 | Visual Basic |
| T1059.006 | Python |
| T1059.007 | JavaScript |
| T1059.008 | Network Device CLI |
| T1059.009 | Cloud API |
| T1059.010 | AutoHotKey |
| T1059.011 | Lua |
| T1059.012 | Hypervisor CLI |
| T1059.013 | Container CLI/API |

How it's typically used:
- Running a one-liner or script to launch a payload (e.g., powershell -enc <base64> or bash -c 'curl … | sh').
- Executing discovery commands, downloading second-stage tools, or establishing persistence.
- Chaining interpreters (e.g., a shell spawning Python) to obscure intent.

Common detections/mitigations:
- Monitor process creation for interpreter binaries with suspicious arguments (encoded commands, -enc, -nop, -w hidden).
- Enable script block logging (PowerShell) and command-line auditing.
- Restrict interpreter availability, use application allowlisting, and enforce constrained language mode.

Note: T1059 covers execution via interpreters. Related techniques include T1053 (Scheduled Task/Job), T1204 (User Execution), and T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation), which describe other execution paths.
